This looks like the ISSP 2014 Citizenship module (or the 2004 Citizenship module), and the US GSS ISSP supplement item on government's right to keep people under video surveillance in public areas. "Can't choose" rates for such items are typically around 3-6%.

[4.5]

This looks like the ISSP National Identity module, where "Can't choose" is an explicit option in the self-completion supplement. For US respondents, this item on "truly American" with effort versus birth typically gets low non-response, though an explicit "can't choose" option raises it slightly above what an implicit DK would produce. I'd estimate roughly 4-5%.

[4.5]

This looks like the ISSP-style module (e.g., ISSP 2021 or similar), with "Can't choose" as an explicit option. For a topic like AI and job loss, the share choosing "Can't choose" is typically low to moderate, since most people have an opinion, though AI is a less familiar subject. In the US, with a self-completion supplement and a neutral midpoint available, I'd estimate roughly 3-5%.

[3.5]

This resembles ISSP-style items (e.g., ISSP Social Inequality or Role of Government). "Can't choose" in the ISSP is typically 2-6% for opinion statements. For an attitudinal item about business leaders making money at expense of ordinary people, there is a neutral middle option, which reduces "can't choose." In the US ISSP, DK rates are generally low, around 2-4%.

[3.0]

This looks like the ISSP-style item, with a "Can't choose" option on a populism statement in a self-completion supplement. In ISSP U.S. data, "can't choose" rates for such attitude items typically run around 3-6%.

[3.5]

This looks like an ISSP-style item (the ISSP self-completion supplement, which includes "Can't choose" and an explicit neither-agree-nor-disagree midpoint). For US respondents on a populism-type statement, "Can't choose" typically runs a few percent. The midpoint absorbs many of the uncertain respondents, so I estimate around 3%.

This looks like the ISSP 2014 Citizenship module (or a similar one), where the government-rights questions on monitoring email and similar surveillance items had "Can't choose" selected by a modest share of respondents. In the US ISSP, "Can't choose" rates for these items were typically around 3-6%.

This looks like ISSP-style items (e.g., ISSP National Identity module) with 'Can't choose' offered, and the US GSS administered these. For the ISSP, "can't choose" rates on attitude statements like this typically run 2-5%. For the US, probably around 3%.

This resembles the ISSP-style self-completion supplement items, where "Can't choose" typically draws a few percent of respondents. The statement is somewhat abstract and ambiguous, so non-response might run a bit above the typical rate. In the US ISSP data, "Can't choose" on attitude items like this usually falls around 3-6%.

This looks like an ISSP-style or ESS-style item; in the ISSP National Identity / Citizenship modules, "Can't choose" rates for immigrant-related attitude items typically run around 3-6% in the US. For the "immigrants take jobs away" item in the ISSP US sample, I estimate about 4%.

This looks like the ISSP-style self-completion supplement (e.g., National Identity module), where a "Can't choose" option is offered. Typical "can't choose" rates for attitudinal items in ISSP are around 2-5% for the US. For a question on preference for native-born over immigrants, the rate is probably about 3%.

This looks like the ISSP Social Inequality module in the US (GSS). In the ISSP, "Can't choose" rates for items like this are typically around 2-5% in the US. The government responsibility item had a relatively low rate, probably around 2-3%.

[2.8]

This item resembles the ISSP National Identity/Citizenship module, where the "Can't choose" option typically draws a few percent of respondents. In the US General Social Survey's ISSP supplement, the share choosing "can't choose" on immigrant items is typically around 2-4%, with the "neither agree nor disagree" middle option absorbing much of the ambivalence. I estimate about 3%.

This looks like the ISSP-style Citizenship/Digital society questions, though this exact wording resembles the US General Social Survey (GSS) self-completion supplement. "Can't choose" rates for attitude statements in such supplements typically run around 3-6%. For a question about willingness to share personal data for discounts, a neutral midpoint is available, so "Can't choose" is likely lower, around 3%.

[3.5]

This looks like ISSP-style items (National Identity module) with a self-completion supplement. "Can't choose" rates in ISSP for US are typically a few percent for attitude items; this abstract item about nations might get somewhat higher, around 4-6%.

[4.5]

This resembles an ISSP-style item on self-rated ability to use the Internet. Most U.S. adults use the Internet, and those who don't would likely select "very bad" or "bad" rather than "can't choose." Still, some non-users and older respondents may pick "can't choose," so I expect a small share.

[1.8]

This looks like the ESS-style left-right scale item administered to a US sample, with "Can't choose" offered explicitly in a self-completion supplement. In ESS countries, "don't know" on this item typically runs about 5-10%, and in the US, where "left/right" terminology is less commonly used, I'd expect it to be higher. With an explicit "Can't choose" option in self-completion, I estimate roughly 10-15%.

[11.5]

This looks like the General Social Survey (GSS) self-completion supplement, or a similar survey with a 0-10 trust scale. Generalized trust items typically have low "don't know" rates, about 1-3%. In a self-completion format with an explicit "Can't choose" option, the rate is probably around 2%.

[2.1]

This is an ISSP National Identity module-style item, with "Can't choose" offered explicitly in the self-completion supplement. In ISSP US data, "can't choose" rates for items like this typically run from a few percent to about 10%. For this question on becoming truly American, I estimate around 4-5%.

[4.5]

This looks like a General Social Survey (GSS) item on AI and jobs, where "Can't choose" is offered as an explicit option. For attitude questions with a middle option plus "Can't choose," that option is usually selected by a small share, around 2-5% of respondents. Because the AI topic is somewhat unfamiliar, the share is probably at the higher end of that range, though the explicit "neither worried nor unworried" option absorbs much of the uncertainty. I estimate roughly 3%.

This looks like the ISSP Citizenship/Role of Government style item (ISSP 2004 Citizenship, US GSS). In the ISSP, "Can't choose" rates for these civil liberties items are typically around 3-6%. For video surveillance in public areas, the US rate was probably around 3%.

[3.5]

This looks like an ISSP-type item (Social Inequality or similar), where "Can't choose" typically gets a few percent. With a neutral midpoint also available, "Can't choose" rates usually run 2-5%. For a US sample on this attitude statement, I estimate around 3%.

[3.0]

This looks like the ISSP-style self-completion items, where "Can't choose" typically draws a few percent on opinion statements. For a fairly accessible statement like this one, the rate is probably around 3-4%, since most respondents have an opinion on conflict between ordinary people and those in power.

[3.5]

This looks like an ISSP 2014 Citizenship module or ISSP 2004... actually the question about government rights to monitor e-mails comes from ISSP Citizenship 2014. In the US, the self-completion supplement had "Can't choose" options. For these items, "Can't choose" rates are typically 3-6%. For the e-mail monitoring item, the percentage is perhaps around 4%.

This looks like an ISSP-style item with a "Can't choose" option in a self-completion supplement. In ISSP US data, "can't choose" rates for opinion items typically run around 2-6%. This item is a bit abstract, so the rate is probably a bit higher, around 4%.

[4.0]

This item comes from populism scales used in ISSP/ESS-style modules, where "can't choose" typically draws around 3-6% on political attitude items. In the ISSP self-completion supplement, "can't choose" rates for populism items tend to run a bit higher than the average for items with a neutral midpoint, but this statement is simple and widely understood, so the rate should be on the lower end of that range.

[3.5]

This resembles the ISSP-style items (e.g., "Immigrants improve society by bringing new ideas and cultures"), where "Can't choose" typically gets about 3-6% in the US. The neutral middle option is also available, which draws off some uncertainty. In the US ISSP 2013/2003 national identity modules, "can't choose" rates for such items were around 3-5%.

[3.5]

This looks like the ISSP Role of Government/Social Inequality module in the US (GSS self-completion supplement). In ISSP, "Can't choose" for income redistribution items typically runs around 2-4% in the US. Because this is a self-completion supplement with an explicit option, the share is modest but non-trivial; the item about government reducing income differences is easy to answer, so I'd estimate about 3%.

[3.0]

This looks like the ISSP-style or the International Social Survey Programme US module, and the "Can't choose" option appears with these attitude items. In ISSP data, "can't choose" rates for immigrant-related items typically run around 2-5%. For the US, the immigrants-take-jobs item sees about 3% "can't choose," and since this is a self-completion supplement the rate is probably a bit lower than in interviewer-administered modes.

[3.0]

This resembles the ISSP National Identity module items in the US General Social Survey, where "can't choose" rates for attitude statements typically run around 2-4%. The statement is clear and familiar, and a neutral midpoint is available, so most respondents who are undecided will pick the midpoint rather than "can't choose". I estimate a rate near the low end of that range.

[2.5]

This looks like the ISSP-style or a Pew/GSS-type privacy item with "Can't choose" offered. In GSS-type self-completion supplements, "Can't choose" rates for attitude statements are typically 2-6%. For this item (willingness to trade personal info for discounts), respondents have a clear opinion generally, but a neutral option exists, so "Can't choose" would be low.

This looks like the ISSP Citizenship module, where the "Can't choose" option is offered for such frequency questions. For political-activity frequency items, the rate of "Can't choose" is typically low, about 1-3%. In the US ISSP, for social media political expression, I estimate around 2%.

In the US ISSP, "can't choose" rates for such attitudinal items tend to be around 3-6%. This item on nations having their own country is somewhat abstract, so it may draw a bit higher DK rates.

This looks like the ISSP-style item on self-rated ability, with "Can't choose" offered. For an Internet-use item, some respondents with no experience may say "can't choose," and in the U.S. a small share of adults don't use the Internet. In a self-completion supplement, "Can't choose" for such items typically runs about 2-4%.

[2.5]

This looks like the ISSP/ GSS-style self-completion supplement with generalized trust on a 0-10 scale. In ISSP-type modules, "can't choose" rates for such items are typically low, around 1-3%. For the US ISSP, the self-completion supplement, "Can't choose" for trust items is likely about 1-2%.

This looks like the ISSP-style (International Social Survey Programme) self-completion supplement, where "Can't choose" is offered as a substantive option. For an attitude item on AI and job displacement, which is a fairly new topic, "Can't choose" rates typically run around 2-5%. A middle option ("neither worried nor unworried") is also offered, which absorbs some uncertainty. I'd estimate about 3%.

This looks like the ISSP National Identity module items, where "Can't choose" is often selected by a modest share of respondents on such questions. For the US ISSP, the "Can't choose" rate on similar items is typically around 3-6%.

In ISSP 2004 items on government rights (e.g., tap telephone, video surveillance), "can't choose" typically ran about 3-6%. For video surveillance in public areas, the rate is probably on the lower side, maybe around 3%.

This resembles an ISSP-style item, probably from the ISSP/GSS self-completion supplement. "Can't choose" rates on such opinion items usually run around 2-5%. For a populist-attitude item like this one, with a neutral midpoint available, I'd estimate roughly 3%.

This resembles ISSP-style items, with "can't choose" offered as an explicit option in a self-completion supplement. For an abstract attitude statement like this one, I'd expect roughly 3-6% of respondents to choose it, and I'll settle on a figure near the middle of that range.

This looks like the ISSP 2014 Citizenship module (or a similar one), where the item on government monitoring of emails has a "Can't choose" option. In the ISSP US data, "Can't choose" rates for such items are typically around 3-6%. For this item in the US (GSS-administered), I estimate about 4%.

For the US ISSP, "Can't choose" rates on attitudinal items like this one typically run around 2-4%. The income-difference item is a well-known, relatively easy question, so I'd expect it to fall at the lower end of that range.

This resembles the ISSP or a similar survey where "Can't choose" is explicitly offered. For an attitude question about providing personal information for discounts, the share choosing "Can't choose" is typically small, maybe 3-6%. Since a neutral midpoint is available, the don't-know share is likely lower, around 3%.

This looks like an ISSP-style question (Citizenship module), where "Can't choose" rates for frequency items are typically small, a few percent. For a behavior question like this one, people usually can answer, so I'd estimate around 1.5%.

This resembles ISSP-style items (ISSP National Identity module), where "can't choose" typically gets a few percent. For an abstract question about nations making their own decisions, US responses for "can't choose" would probably run around 3-5%.

This looks like ISSP-style item (Digital/Internet skills). "Can't choose" for internet ability would be chosen mostly by people who never use the internet, perhaps 3-5% in the US. In the US, about 90% use the internet; non-users might say can't choose or very bad. I estimate around 3%.

This is the ESS-style left-right scale item. In the ESS, "don't know" rates for left-right placement are typically around 5-10% in many countries. For the US, with in-person/telephone and a self-completion supplement offering "Can't choose" explicitly, the rate would likely be higher than in the main interview, since Americans are less familiar with left-right terminology than with liberal-conservative. I estimate around 10%.
